subject: physics_2
question_text: Discuss Bohr's theory of the spectrum of hydrogen atom?

mark_split.label: The transition rule and Rydberg's formula

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. SOURCE DEFECT CORRECTED: under "Lyman Series" the book prints "This series lies in the ultra violet region which is the visible region" — the sentence contradicts itself. The Lyman series is ULTRAVIOLET; the VISIBLE series is Balmer, which the book itself states correctly in the next paragraph. The card writes the physics correctly and records the book's wording in that step's why. The book's own energy-level figure also mis-spells the series as "Blamer", "Bracket" and "Pfund" run together; the spellings are corrected here. Physics hand-checked with 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹: Lyman n₁ = 1 gives 912 Å to 1216 Å (ultraviolet); Balmer n₁ = 2 gives 3646 Å to 6563 Å (visible); Paschen n₁ = 3, Brackett n₁ = 4 and Pfund n₁ = 5 all lie beyond 8000 Å (infrared).

recall_prompt: Say the transition rule and Rydberg's formula, then name each series with its final orbit and its region of the spectrum.

steps.label: The transition rule
steps.mark_note: hν = E₂ − E₁ and Rydberg's formula
lines: When the electron moves from an outer orbit n₂
to an inner orbit n₁, the atom emits a photon:
The wavelength of each line follows from Bohr's
constant. Each value of n₁ gives one series.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both equations: the photon condition and the wavelength formula.
steps.why: Bohr's energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. Subtracting two of them and dividing by hc turns the level diagram into a wavelength formula, which is what makes the spectrum a set of separate lines rather than a band.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/λ = R(1/n₂² − 1/n₁²). The smaller n comes first, or λ comes out negative.
Leaving out the value of R. The constant is part of the formula mark.

recall.must_convey: That a photon of energy hν = E₂ − E₁ is emitted and 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²).
accept: h nu equals E two minus E one
one by lambda equals R into one by n one squared minus one by n two squared

steps.memory_tip: Smaller n first inside the bracket, or the wavelength comes out negative.

steps.label: The energy level diagram
steps.margin_note: Levels for n = 1, 2, 3 and ∞, with one Lyman arrow down to n = 1 and one Balmer arrow down to n = 2.
steps.why: The spacing is drawn to scale from Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so the picture itself shows why the drop to n = 1 is by far the largest — that is the whole reason the Lyman series is ultraviolet.
common_mistakes: Drawing the levels equally spaced. They crowd together towards n = ∞.

recall.must_convey: That an energy level diagram is drawn with arrows coming down to n = 1 for Lyman and to n = 2 for Balmer.
accept: arrows down to n equals one and n equals two

steps.memory_tip: Levels crowd at the top; the gap down to n = 1 is the biggest on the page.

steps.label: Lyman series
lines: Lyman series: the electron moves to the first
This series lies in the ultraviolet region
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Final orbit n₁ = 1, and the region is ULTRAVIOLET.
steps.why: The book prints "This series lies in the ultra violet region which is the visible region" — the sentence contradicts itself. Lyman is ultraviolet; the visible series is Balmer, which the book states correctly in the very next paragraph. The n = 1 level lies 10.2 eV below n = 2, and a 10.2 eV photon is far outside the visible band.
common_mistakes: Calling the Lyman series visible. It is ultraviolet — the eye cannot detect it.
Writing n₂ = 1, 2, 3. The outer orbit must be above the inner one, so n₂ starts at 2.

recall.must_convey: That Lyman transitions end on n₁ = 1 and the series is ultraviolet.
accept: electron comes to the first orbit
it lies in the ultraviolet region
reject: it lies in the visible region

steps.memory_tip: Lyman ends on 1 and is the only ultraviolet series.

steps.label: Balmer series
lines: Balmer series: the electron moves to the second
This series lies in the visible region
(6563 Å down to the limit at 3646 Å).
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Final orbit n₁ = 2, and this is the VISIBLE series.
steps.why: Balmer is the series the eye can detect, and the red 6563 Å line (n₂ = 3) is the one seen in a hydrogen discharge tube. This is the series the book's Lyman paragraph confuses with Lyman.
common_mistakes: Writing n₁ = 3 for Balmer. That is the Paschen series.
Saying the whole series is red. Only the first line is red; the rest run towards violet.

recall.must_convey: That Balmer transitions end on n₁ = 2 and the series is visible.
accept: electron comes to the second orbit
it lies in the visible region
reject: it lies in the infrared region

steps.memory_tip: Balmer ends on 2 and is the only series the eye can see.

steps.label: The infrared transitions
steps.margin_note: The upper levels only: Paschen comes down to n = 3, Brackett to n = 4. Pfund comes down to n = 5.
steps.why: The upper levels sit close together, so the drops between them are small, the photon energies are low and every one of these series lies in the infrared.
common_mistakes: Drawing these arrows down to n = 1. Each infrared series has its own final orbit.

recall.must_convey: That arrows are drawn down to n = 3 for Paschen and down to n = 4 for Brackett.
accept: draw arrows to n equals three and n equals four
reject: arrows down to n equals one

steps.memory_tip: Close levels, small drops, long waves — everything above n = 3 is infrared.

steps.label: The infrared series
lines: All three lie in the infrared region.

lines.text: n₁ = 1 UV · n₁ = 2 visible · n₁ ≥ 3 infrared

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Three series, each with its final orbit, all infrared.
steps.why: Above n = 3 the levels are so close that every transition between them releases less than 1.5 eV, which is below the red end of the visible band — so Paschen, Brackett and Pfund are all infrared.
common_mistakes: Naming only Paschen. The question asks for the spectrum, so all the series are wanted.
Putting Brackett at n₁ = 3. Paschen is 3, Brackett is 4, Pfund is 5.

recall.must_convey: That Paschen ends on n₁ = 3, Brackett on n₁ = 4, Pfund on n₁ = 5, and all three are infrared.
accept: Brackett fourth orbit, Pfund fifth orbit

steps.memory_tip: Count the final orbits in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund.

insider_note: The book's own Lyman paragraph says the ultraviolet region "is the visible region" — write ultraviolet for Lyman and visible for Balmer, and the marks are safe.
